I was on my Mac this morning, just minding my own business, when suddenly I found myself using the Linux laptop, and I liked it.
On Sunday mornings, I do system maintenance. This means running updates on all my computers. Right now, that's five machines: one Linux desktop, two Linux laptops, one Mac desktop, and one Mac laptop. Yes, that's too many, but it is what it is.

While typing on the Framework, the first thing I thought about was how much I prefer typing on it to typing on the MacBook Air. Then I remembered how much I like the idea of Linux. Then I noticed that Emacs starts up more than twice as fast on the Framework for some reason. Then I remembered that the best (and only) way to have consistent Emacs key bindings on Linux is to, well, use Emacs.
All this to say that the conflict between running macOS, Linux, or both is still a thing. As troublesome and complex as it can be, I think the answer will always be "both". Surely I can manage it, right? Maybe if I only use the laptops for simple things like blogging, browsing, or journaling, things will be easy enough. I'll never be able to settle on one or the other. Just admit it.
I'm on the couch typing this in Emacs using the Framework, both things I told myself a week ago that I'd stop doing. My stupid brain is always mucking things up.

articles.description:
David Pape asked:




I just typed



>Closes: #47, #48, #49, #50, #51, #52, #53, #54



into a commit description, all by hand.



Is there a way in Emacs to expand some kind of range description to make this easier? 😅



I want to expand strings like "5-10, 15-18, 3" into numbers.




Hmm, could be useful. It reminds me of how page ranges work, which will be handy if I want to tinker with PDFs. Let's see if something like this works:




(defun sacha-parse-page-range (s)
  "Parse a page range string and return a list of numbers.
Ex: 1-5
2-4, 6-10
1 4 7-9
3-11/2   - this one specifies an increment"
  (seq-mapcat
   (lambda (part)
     (let ((nums (mapcar 'string-to-number (split-string part " *[-/] *"))))
       (if (= (length nums) 1)
           nums
         (number-sequence (elt nums 0) (elt nums 1) (elt nums 2)))))
   (split-string s "[, \t\n\r]+")))

(ert-deftest sacha-parse-page-range ()
  (should (equal (sacha-parse-page-range "5-10")
                 '(5 6 7 8 9 10)))
  (should (equal (sacha-parse-page-range "1-5, 8")
                 '(1 2 3 4 5 8)))
  (should (equal (sacha-parse-page-range "1 4 7-9")
                 '(1 4 7 8 9)))
  (should (equal (sacha-parse-page-range "3-11/2")
                 '(3 5 7 9 11))))

(defun sacha-issue-range (range)
  "Expand RANGE to a list of issues and insert them."
  (interactive "MRange (ex: 1-5, 7): ")
  (let ((s (mapconcat (lambda (n) (format "#%d" n))
                      (sacha-parse-page-range range)
                      ", ")))
    (when (called-interactively-p 'any)
      (insert s))
    s))

This is part of my EmacsConfiguration.

That said, listening to music in such a way is largely a passive activity, where your main focus is somewhere else. The better music players that acknowledge this difference in focus provide mechanisms for remote-controlling them from other apps. So it is with the Triode app for macOS, which leverages Cocoa frameworks (App Intents in particular) to support remote control.
triode.el is an Emacs Lisp library which provides a simple remote control interface to the Triode app. Basic support for selecting a radio station, play/stop, and muting are provided. Not every feature in the Triode app is accessible to triode.el though; this is controlled by the App Intents actually implemented by its developer, The Iconfactory.

Interested readers can learn more about triode.el in its user guide.
triode.el is now available on MELPA. This release joins my other packages that support remote control of music apps on macOS from Emacs:
now-playing.el - Interface for the Music app.
shazam.el - Interface for Shazam music recognition.
All the above efforts have been an exploration of malleable computing using Emacs as the main orchestration tool. I plan on posting a more technical deep dive reflecting this work in the not too distant future. That said, if you’re a macOS user who uses Emacs and Triode, I encourage you to give triode.el a try. Also, consider this a plug for Triode app, a well-designed app that does a great job of taking advantage of the Cocoa frameworks to provide internet radio across different devices provided by Apple.

articles.description:
What’s the future of Emacs? He asks that question in the context of assuming that Emacs will continue to exist for any timeline that matters to us. But how, he asks, will we use it?


The answer that will occur to most of us is speech mediated input á la Star Trek TNG. We’ll simply tell Emacs what we want it to do and it will do it. But think about that for a moment. Would you really want to dictate the code for your latest program to the computer? Or would you even want to dictate your documentation, story, or letter to your computer?


Sure, you could say something like, “Computer write a program to do such and such.” but then you’re not using Emacs at all. The same for asking the computer to write something for you. That—more or less—is here today but most of us don’t like the results and, again, we’re not really using Emacs in those situations.


For my part, my written thoughts are always much better organized than my spoken ones so even with  capable voice input, I’d much prefer to use the keyboard. Maiorana agrees. He points back to a couple of episodes from Tales From the Darkside1 in which people use the keyboard to do magic with the computer. For him, Meta+x is the spell that enables the magic and he’s very attached to it. Like me, he doesn’t anticipate abandoning the keyboard.


What do you think? Will we still use the keyboard or will we move on to something better?

Earlier this year I added Ghostel to my
Emacs configuration. Ghostel is a terminal emulator for Emacs that uses
Ghostty's engine underneath. It is a delight to use
especially with the TUI applications.
Nested Emacs frame problem
I use Emacs in daemon
mode,
and then use emacsclient to open new frames from the daemon. To use the same
Emacs daemon when opening files through other programs such as git, sops, I have
a small shell script ee configured as my default EDITOR. It opens a new
Emacs frame in the terminal.
#!/bin/sh

exec emacsclient --create-frame --no-window-system "$@"

When I run this script from Ghostel, it opens a nested Emacs frame in Ghostel's
terminal session.

Solution
Emacs sets an environment variable INSIDE_EMACS for shells and subprocesses.
The script use this variable to check if it is launched from Ghostel and use the
--reuse-frame flag to open the new buffer in the current frame.
#!/bin/sh

if [ "$INSIDE_EMACS" = "ghostel" ]
then
  exec emacsclient --reuse-frame "$@"
fi

exec emacsclient --create-frame --no-window-system "$@"
articles.title: Ankit Gadiya: Fix nested Emacs frames

What it does is insert words and phrases into the current buffer "to

articles.description:
org-todo is C-c
C-t.  Today I learned about another command with a similar
keybinding (C-c C-x C-t) --
org-toggle-timestamp-overlays.  Note the C-x
in the middle.



When I pressed that key combination (inadvertently), all the
YYYY-MM-DD timestamps in the buffer were converted to the MM/DD/YYYY
format.  This was unacceptable -- I needed to change them back.
However undo did not revert the timestamps; it just undid
the last edit.  Furthermore, these undesired timestamps couldn't be
edited and were impervious to org-shiftright.  I was
confused yet again.



I didn't even know how this happened.  So I
invoked view-lossage as a kind reader once suggested 1
and discovered org-toggle-timestamp-overlays.



The docstring was no help – it's self-evident that it would "Toggle
the use of custom time stamp formats."  Eager to clock out of my task,
I didn't care to learn more.  All I wanted to do was undo the effect.



I figured that since it toggles the timestamp, all I had to do was
invoke it again to toggle it back.  Nope.  Well, a nice message
appears, saying "Time stamp overlays removed."  Yet the timestamps
looked the same.



Undaunted, I figured I'd reload the buffer with org-mode-restart.
That had no effect.  To finally fix this, I deleted the buffer and
revisited the file.



A command like this surely is in the same category as upcase-region,
which is disabled by default.  And so this is why I added
  (put 'org-toggle-timestamp-overlays 'disabled t) to my init file.



  1 See https://ray-on-emacs.blogspot.com/2026/05/emacs-view-commands.html
articles.title: Raymond Zeitler: Now org-toggle-timestamp-overlays is Disabled

Ctrl+c r to invoke org-capture because that was what I was used to with remember-mode.


Although I’m sure there are some, I can’t think of any reason to use remember-mode these days. Org mode can do everything it can and more. Org’s templates make capturing data and notes so much easier and, of course, you can bring all the other Org tools to bear on the results.


BBSnek uses it for quick notes—and it’s great for that—but Org can do that too and so much more. The truth is, I’m surprised that anyone is still using it for any other reason than inertia. Still, as usual, Emacs lets us have it our way and for those who prefer the simpler and lighter weight remember-mode, it’s there for them.

articles.description:
Aquí, is sort of a niche application but is potentially useful for more than just its intended use.


The back story is that Choi really likes the sunrise-sunset command in Emacs that tells him the times that the sun rises and sets. The problem is that sunrise-sunset requires that you first specify the latitude and longitude of where you want to know the times. The standard way of doing that is to record them in your init.el, which is what I do. Choi, however, travels with his laptop but still wants to know when the sun is coming up or going down. There’s no automatic way of setting the information so he wrote Aquí to provide it. The only downside is that it works exclusively on the Mac platform.


Once installed, all you need do is call aqui to set all the appropriate information. I hardly ever travel these days so I wasn’t going to bother but it’s easy to use and can give you your current latitude and longitude as well as your address so I thought, “Why not?”. After I installed and ran it, it gave me my exact address as well as my latitude and longitude. That might sometimes vary a bit depending on the vagaries of GPS but it’s certain to be close.


If you decide to try it out, be sure to take a look at the user manual so see what commands are available. Mostly, though, you’ll just need to run aqui. Also be sure to check out the installation section because you need to install a shortcut. That’s just a matter of clicking on a link in the manual but Aquí won’t work until you do.
articles.title: Irreal: Aquí Location Finder

A few days ago I announced
that I am working on denote-data. The goal is to provide an opt-in,
in-memory cache for Denote. It can be used to speed up certain
computationally expensive operations. It must be opt-in because there
are many users, myself included, who do not need such functionality (I
program because the challenge is fun, just how I did with denote-sequence, for example).
I have a final update on this that I posted on denote.git issue 724 
and am copying below. Any future changes will appear in the release
notes of the next version of Denote. In short: it is happening.
The status update on denote.git
Hello again folks!
I have an update on the denote-data project. The code is in this denote.git branch for now: https://github.com/protesilaos/denote/tree/denote-data
What I am doing:
Find the computationaly heavy functions.
Write denote-data variants for them.
Introduce variables to funcall VAR instead of calling the heavy functions directly.
Make the denote-data-mode set those variables.
This way we can have any extension do what denote-data does. And this way denote-data can be its own package as well.
The first big problem I see now is how to make the caching functions async. I will figure this out by studying list-packages and related.
Then I want to study filenotify.el. @mentalisttraceur I have noted that your code is okay for copyright purposes, so I can check it out. Or you can send a PR, if you prefer.
Otherwise, I think this is almost done.
With an opt-in cache we can support other workflows that people have been asking for, such as in-buffer completion.

articles.description:
One of my favorite Emacs commands is sunrise-sunset (Sunrise/Sunset (GNU Emacs Manual)) to get the day’s times for sunrise and sunset. For it to work right, you must have Emacs pre-configured with location information. This is done by setting three customizable variables:
calendar-latitude
calendar-longitude
calendar-location-name
If you run Emacs on a system that is fixed in location, manually setting the above variables is a one time task. However if you do a fair amount of traveling with Emacs on a laptop, a more programmatic solution might be desired using a location service, ideally an OS-native one. If you’re a macOS user, Aquí (aqui.el) does just that by invoking a Shortcut to query the OS-native location service.
Leveraging Shortcuts gives Emacs access to a high-accuracy fused location update without need to build, install, and configure a separate macOS executable.
Once Aquí is installed, updating the location is done via the aqui command.


1

M-x aqui RET





This will update the above mentioned variables and message the current location in the mini-buffer.
For more information, refer to the Aquí User Guide.
Aquí is now available on MELPA.

wrote back in July, although I’ve had Embark installed for some time, I’ve only just begun to really use it. Most of my uses involve following a link (of any type) and acting on a group of files, typically to delete several files at once. Of course, those uses are barely scratching the surface of Embark’s capabilities.


Those capabilities are essentially open ended. By that I mean you can define your own Embark actions. Stefano Rodighiero has a nice example of this. It’s a nice example for two reasons. First, it’s simple and easy to follow even though—the second reason—I don’t know anything about what he’s trying to do.  The point is that Rodighiero has an obscure—to me—application that he wants to provide an action for but you don’t need to know the details of the application to follow the action.


This is incredibly powerful. Rodighiero let Embark do the hard work of identifying and parsing the target and merely wrote some simple glue to take that target reference and do something useful with it.


If, like me, you’re just beginning to feel your way around Embark, Rodighiero’s post is a useful read. You almost certainly won’t have a need to copy his action but it’s an excellent go by for your own.
articles.title: Irreal: A Nice Example Of An Embark Action

articles.description:
The argument against the Atlanta Dream says their transition-heavy style might be incompatible with playoff basketball. But in the three playoff games they’ve played so far, the latest a 92-82 home win over New York to open the second round, Karl Smesko's team has totally set the terms. As they see it, this is playoff basketball: fast, tireless, always connected. 
Even when the Dream bump into issues running their halfcourt offense, they make the math work for them in other ways. The best offensive rebounder in league history wins them extra possessions, and a team defense that’s forced more turnovers than any other WNBA team this year sets up easy scoring opportunities against defenses on their heels. That made them a nightmare first-round matchup for the Washington Mystics, who turned the ball over more than any other WNBA team this year. Washington’s season indeed ended thanks to a 42-15 turnover differential across two games.
Lest that stat be blamed on the young Mystics’ nerves, consider the 32 points Atlanta scored off 21 turnovers from veteran-stocked New York in Sunday's game. The fix for Game 2 on Wednesday sounds easy: Don’t turn the ball over. But the Atlanta Dream are a team designed to make it difficult. The Liberty’s problems weren’t all self-inflicted.
articles.title: The Atlanta Dream Can Poke And Prod You To Death

articles.author: Kelsey McKinney
articles.description:
PHILADELPHIA — When the lights went out, a crisp, adolescent shriek rose from all sides of the arena, anticipating her arrival. But she did not come, not just yet. Instead, a silence fell heavy and unsettled where the shrieking had been, as if making space for the ball at the other end of the arena, descending ever so slowly, blinking blue, pulsing as if it were alive. More than 40,000 eyes fixated on the descending orb. It was round, but not a perfect sphere, with bumps and craters on its surface like a morning star weapon with all of its spikes truncated, or a children’s bumble ball powder coated in black. 
Though I was on the other side of the arena, and thousands of people were between me and the ball, it was dark, and there was nothing but air to separate us. I looked at the ball the way I look at the moon: with an awe bordering on reverence. Then it followed the same slow path back up into the rafters, and for a little while, I forgot about it. 
On the main stage a large half-circle dome rested atop the space where Phoebe Bridgers would eventually emerge, like the kind of mesh tents that protect food from the bites of prowling bugs. As the ball on one side of the arena disappeared, the tent on the other lit up. The shrieks began again. And then it lifted, lights gleaming from the edge of it straight down so that Bridgers' black dress was awash in so much light that it looked gray, and the whole dome had the appearance of a UFO lifting off the ground in a movie.
articles.title: Phoebe Bridgers Showed Us How To See In The Dark

articles.author: Israel Daramola
articles.description:
I'm not sure when we fell into the collective delusion that first-round quarterbacks should be capable of leading an NFL team on Day 1. Was it induced by the take economy? Is this sports radio's fault? Did Joe Burrow's early success create this standard? I can understand certain teams like the Browns or Jets believing it necessary to have their top draft pick run the offense right away, because they have little hope otherwise, but what's everyone else's excuse? While you may get Andrew Luck or Lamar Jackson on occasion, often these teams just end up stunting the growth of potential stars, who end up having to rehab their careers and abilities elsewhere.
I was thinking about these things Sunday night while watching Bryce Young have arguably the best game of his career for the Carolina Panthers, against the Detroit Lions. Young led the Panthers to a 32-26 win while throwing for 329 yards and two touchdowns on 29-of-41 passing. Second-year wide receiver Tetairoa McMillan was the biggest beneficiary, accounting for 43 percent of the Panthers' total yardage. He caught 14 passes for 192 yards, and accounted for those two TD passes.
Young and McMillan's chemistry has been building since last season, and never was it more useful than when last night's game was on the line. Despite outplaying the Lions for most of the game, the Panthers were in a spot of trouble late in the fourth quarter. After Detroit scored and cut the lead to six, Young and the offense took over on their own 36-yard line with 3:38 left to play. At the very least, the Panthers needed to get a first down and force a few timeouts out of the Lions. A one-yard run by Chuba Hubbard forced the first burned timeout, and then a penalty followed by an incompletion put Young in a tough spot. Suddenly it was third-and-14, only 22 seconds had come off the clock, and Young was scrambling to avoid pressure. That's when he saw McMillan near the sideline, and made an absurd throw to invite an incredible catch:
articles.title: Patience Is Paying Off For Bryce Young

articles.description:
The first line in a Min Jin Lee novel gives you the whole story. In Free Food For Millionaires, it’s “Competence can be a curse.” In her follow-up, Pachinko, it’s “History has failed us, but no matter.” Both establish the thesis and themes of the novels, and of her larger project of writing about the Korean diasporic experience. 
The first line of Lee’s latest novel, American Hagwon, does the same: “The rules of engagement have changed already.” The novel, which came out last week nearly a decade after Pachinko was published, situates her characters—and by extension, the Korean diaspora—at a point of transition where they must adapt. Ever concerned with the financial realities of Korean families, in American Hagwon, Lee considers the cost, both economic and human, of a people striving to elevate itself.
American Hagwon tells the story of a community centered around a hagwon founded in Los Angeles by Korean immigrants. Hagwons are cram schools that are incredibly popular in South Korea, and in the U.S. among Korean communities. They exist to supplement the day-to-day education students get at school. Students often attend them every day after school and late into the night, doing extra work to get ahead academically and to prepare for the highly competitive exams required for admission to the top Korean universities, as well as elite American universities.
articles.title: The Case Against Exceptionalism

articles.author: Ray Ratto
articles.description:
The Atlanta Braves are not the best team in this postseason, but there do seem to be more of them than anyone else. Manager Walt Weiss has appeared blithely unconcerned by the math that demonstrates that the more pitching changes a team makes, the greater the likelihood that some of them will turn to shit.
And yet Weiss persists, because these are the tools that have been provided for him. After the attrition of the regular season, he has at his disposal three discernible starting pitchers; the best of those, Chris Sale, already had to close out one game against the Phillies in Atlanta's wild-card win, and has not yet started in the team's NLDS. In a more normal environment, this "all hands on deck" strategy would be pointing toward a very predictable outcome: a mutiny by the crew.
But Sunday was the acme of that plan to date. The Braves beat the Dodgers, 3-2, in Game 2 of the National League Division Series, because of stellar work by a 32-year-old ultra-journeyman whose career has been dominated by surgery rehab, and a 21-year-old puppy who fetches whatever is thrown his way because that's what 21-year-olds get to do this time of year. More or less everyone in the Atlanta bullpen was called upon to contribute to the team's most important game of the year so far, and more or less everyone did.
articles.title: Atlanta’s Least Heralded Relievers Did The Most

articles.description:
Who among us has not floated the idea of starting a bookstore to our friends and partners, as a way out of the nightmare that is 9-to-5 work and LinkedIn hell? In 2021, Lucy Yu actually did it. She had been unhappily working as a chemical engineer and socking away money, and when she had $40,000 saved, she took the plunge and opened Yu & Me Books, the first Asian American woman-owned bookstore in New York City.
Yu & Me Books was the fantasy embodied. It was a cozy space in Chinatown, filled with Yu's favorite books and new releases, and she hosted author and community events each week. But that fantasy was only possible because Lucy was pushing her body and mind to the absolute limit of what she could handle. Everything changed when a fire nearly destroyed her shop in 2023. I've been a fan and supporter of Yu & Me since it first opened, but I was curious to talk with Lucy about how the fire forced her to learn that in order to take care of her community, she had to learn to take care of herself first.

Are you grasping for an explanation of the Jacksonville Jaguars' typically excellent performance? Look no further than the Microsoft Surface. Microsoft Surface tablets are in the hands of all the Jaguars coaches on the sidelines now, and players are allowed to look at them as well. You can even buy a Jacksonville Jaguars skin to customize your own Microsoft Surface at home. 
With Microsoft Surface, the opposing team can no longer hide behind their helmets. A few clicks or swipes of the virtual keyboard brings up all the information about them that was heretofore concealed. That includes photographs of the faces of each player, their height, weight, and colleges attended. Where past generations of football teams may have focused on developing better footballs or shoulder pads, the Microsoft Surface delivers the Jacksonville Jaguars the most powerful differentiator in the modern NFL: information. 
Data unearthed by Microsoft Surface can be relayed by coaches directly into earpieces in the helmets of each Jacksonville Jaguar. Then a defensive lineman, for example, can look across at the offensive lineman on the other team and say, "Your facemask no longer intimidates me. You are Dalton Risner. You attended Kansas State University. Your favorite food is chocolate. I can tell you the exact address of your parents and other loved ones. A team of assassins is sitting outside of their homes, as we speak. The choice before you now is simple. Either you allow me to run past you, or you will never see them again." Then the Jaguars player could describe in detail what their houses look like on Google Maps. Dalton Risner doesn't know if the other guy is telling the truth, or if the assistant coach just fed him all that information from the sidelines. But does he want to take the chance?
articles.title: Jaguars Junction: Week 4

For more than a year, journalists Maggie Haberman and Jonathan Swan had been trying — and largely failing — to raise awareness about the very strange story of Donald Trump and his aide Natalie Harp. She was not from “a wealthy family,” he said. “This was her dream and it was taken away from her at a young age in just a horrific fashion.”
But according to some on the right, Doe has not suffered enough for reporting her alleged a…

How hard is it to enjoy your husband’s company? According to content made for Christian conservative women, the heaviest cross they may bear is learning to feel affection for their spouses — or at least fake it well enough to buy some peace at home. That’s what I learned perusing the growing field of influencers offering would-be tradwives advice on how to make MAGA marriages work. 
“Normalize liking your husband,” reads a T-shirt sold by Savanna Stone, a 21-year-old self-proclaimed marriage expert who has been selling content preaching marital submission with the backing of shady far-right funders. At first blush, that may seem like a trifling concept. But, as Stone makes clear in her video content, her definition of liking or even loving a husband is both laborious and ascetic to an extr…

Much like our nation itself, the World Cup run for the U.S. men’s national soccer team started off promisingly, only to become a sick joke. The USMNT got eliminated from the 2026 Cup on Monday night after Belgium crushed it 4-1, in a game where the home team was thoroughly outplayed, outclassed and outcoached. But if the loss itself stung, the context in which it was played only made it feel that much worse.  

Yes, that backstory includes Donald Trump, but to a small degree, it also involves USMNT poster child and possible Trump fanboy Christian Pulisic. The first man disgraced the team off the field. The second man disgraced the team on it. How did all of this come to pass? Well, I suppose it’s my job to explain it, although the prospect of doing so excites about as much as having my leg…
articles.title: It's easy to blame the USMNT's World Cup crashout on one man. So I will.

articles.description: The one thing that Washington, D.C., has always had going for it is its beauty. The people who run America from this town have always been an unsightly bunch, but they’ve done their nasty work in a city that has acquired, over the course of this country’s lifespan, an aesthetic like no other. No other major American city looks as regally beautiful as D.C. You and I have a long-standing federal law to thank for this, but we also have a collection of national landmarks clustered in the center of the district that the aforementioned law was written to both protect and to showcase. The Capitol. The Lincoln Memorial. The Washington Monument. These are gorgeous edifices, ones designed to outlast old generations and to inspire newer ones. They are the best of D.C., and therefore the best of Ameri…

If you’re wondering whether there are any good people remaining in the tech sector, or in this country’s ruling class in general, you’d be hard pressed to find a better case study than Craig Newmark. Newmark founded Craigslist.org in San Francisco way back in 1996 and became the sort of accidental billionaire that the early dot-com boom cranked out with seeming regularity. Some of those billionaires went on to become evil (Mark Zuckerberg), and some of them ended up merely becoming rich loud guys (Mark Cuban). Newmark, who ceded his CEO duties at Craigslist shortly after its founding, has endeavored to keep a lower profile, and a lower net worth, than any of them.

To wit: Newmark no longer works with Craigslist at all, and spends the bulk of his time tending to various philanthropic endea…

Wildfires are once again eating their way across California. Three fires, one near Big Sur, one enveloping Lassen and Sierra counties and one raging in Humboldt County, have burned tens of thousands of acres of land, poisoned endangered condors, and closed off various highways and state parks indefinitely. The aforementioned fires have barely been contained by authorities. When (or, *shudder*, if) the fires die down, more fires will follow in their wake. And more after that, and more after that. Wildfire is a natural part of California’s environment, and thanks to humankind’s disastrous warping of the planet’s climate, fires will only grow more widespread and destructive in the years to come.

articles.description: Come with me now to Palo Alto. We’re hopping in the car to make the more than 30-mile drive south of San Francisco to the bucolic campus of Stanford University, where former NFL star Andrew Luck awaits us. The Stanford campus remains as gorgeous, and sheltered, as ever. This is the ideal setting for gifted minds to construct their own realities, and Luck remains one of the more gifted minds that the sport of football has ever produced. Smart enough to read the most complicated defenses at a glance, and smart enough to leave the NFL when he realized that the life of a pro quarterback was making both him, and his wife Nicole, miserable. If these gentlemen, Jacob Coxon and Evan Hubinger, are correct in their assessment, the beginning of our destruction may well have commenced a month ago right here in San Francisco.

The first shot fired in this looming war happened at a seemingly innocuous Cow Hollow storefront known as Andon Market. Back in August, Luna, the AI bot that serves as that store’s manager, fired one of its own employees. The employee in question was dinged by their virtual boss for being late to work, abandoning their post once they got there, and charging snacks…

Quick: name the best croissant filling. If you’re a basic American like me, you only encounter basic croissant flavors: chocolate, almond, and ham and cheese. These are the norm, and they do the job well if you’re hungry and want to feel 10% more French. But surely, you’ve thought, there must be room for more fillings than that in the American croissant repertoire. Surely there must be a, like, fourth thing we can put into one. 

Reader, I’m pleased to report that I have found one such worthy croissant filling, and it’s nothing you’d guess off the top of your head. But take one bite of it, and you’ll know I’m right. 

The croissant in question is dubbed “brown butter cornmeal twice-baked,” and the bakery that sells it is San Francisco’s Butter & Crumble, owned by chef and self-dubbed “girl…
articles.title: I found one of America's best croissants in San Francisco

I imagine it so, so hard: packed stadiums, crowds numbering five figures going wild as I take my shirt off, shady managers hanging out backstage ready to ply me with Hefty bags full of pharmaceutical cocaine. But it’s too late for me, on the cusp of 50, to actually become a rock star — it certainly couldn’t be a skill or charisma issue, no sir — which is why there’s a tiny slice of the hospitality industry that exists to make patrons like me FEEL like rock stars, if only for a brief moment. 

This is where the legendary Phoenix Hotel, plopped down on Eddy Street right in the middle of San Francisco’s Tenderloin neighborhood, comes in.

articles.description:
There’s a good chance you’ve heard of Tadich Grill, given that the restaurant is older than San Francisco itself. It’s existed in one form or another since 1849, when it opened under the name Coffee Stand. That was one year before the city of San Francisco was formally incorporated, and 118 years before the restaurant moved to its current location on California Street in the Financial District. Tadich has been doling out fresh seafood and mesquite-grilled slabs of meat to patrons through a lifespan that has included multiple earthquakes, two world wars, Prohibition and multiple pandemics. It’s not merely the oldest restaurant in San Francisco, but in all of California. An eternal landmark. I only needed to walk through its doors on an early evening this August to understand why.

Actually,…
